standard_text: Use variables to represent two quantities in a proportional relationship in a real-world problem; write an equation to express one quantity, the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.

progression.narrative: 6.RP.5 asks students to run a proportional relationship through all three of its representations — table, equation, graph — and to know which quantity drives which. The logic starts with roles: before any math, a student must name the independent variable (the input they control) and the dependent variable (the output that responds) in a real-world situation (S1). Tables come next, because a table is the rate made visible: every y is the same multiplier times its x, and completing a table (S2) forces the multiply-across habit that additive shortcuts fake. Once the constant multiplier is felt in the rows, it gets a name and a home: the equation y = px, first read out of a completed table (S3), then written straight from the words of a situation and used to answer far-away questions the table can't reach (S4). The graph is the third face of the same relationship — ordered pairs from the table, plotted independent-first, landing on a straight line through the origin (S5). Finally the standard's (E) essential demand matures into judgment: given competing equations for a situation, test them against real values and explain which one is truly proportional and why the other fails (S6).

steps.rationale: The standard opens with 'use variables to represent two quantities' — before writing anything, a student must know which quantity is the independent variable and which is the dependent one. Every later equation places these two roles on specific sides of the equals sign.

Tables are the standard's first analysis tool. Completing a proportional table forces the core insight — every y is the SAME multiplier times its x — and exposes the additive shortcut that fails when x-values skip.

The heart of the standard: compress the table's pattern into one equation, y = px, expressing the dependent variable in terms of the independent one. The division that finds p (y over x, never x over y) is where the work lives.

The full real-world demand: name the variables, write y = px straight from the words, and use the equation to answer questions a table would take pages to reach. This is where the equation earns its keep.

The standard's third representation. Table rows become ordered pairs, pairs become points, and points reveal the signature of proportionality — a straight line through the origin — tying graph, table, and equation together.

The standard's analysis demand at full depth: judge competing equations for a situation by testing values, and explain why an additive or flipped equation cannot represent a proportional relationship.

skills.name: Recall multiplication and division facts fluently

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply and divide within 144 from memory

skills.i_do_script: A stuck fact can be rebuilt instead of guessed from a nearby friendly fact: 7 x 6 is 7 x 5 plus one more 7, so 35 + 7 = 42 -- and the ratio tables in this standard are exactly that picture, one more group each row. Every proportional relationship in this standard runs on one multiplication fact repeated over and over — $6 per cup means 6, 12, 18, 24. If the facts aren't automatic, the tables and equations fall apart. Watch me with 6 x 7: I know 6 x 7 = 42 because 6 x 6 = 36 and one more 6 makes 42. Use a fact you trust to reach the one you don't.

canonical_error.pattern: Cannot recall multiplication or division facts, so every table row and every equation check becomes a fresh struggle
canonical_error.example: Filling a table for y = 7x, the student writes 7, 14, 21, 27 -- they added 6 instead of 7 because 7 x 4 wasn't automatic
canonical_error.why: Facts weren't automatized in grades 3-4. The student understands the proportional pattern but can't execute it reliably, so errors look like reasoning mistakes when they're really recall mistakes.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on — let's check that fact.
redirect_script.prompt: Start from a fact you're sure of. You know 7 x 3 = 21, so 7 x 4 is just one more group of 7. Count up: 21, 28. Write the fact you used next to your answer.
redirect_script.praise: You used a fact you trusted to build the one you needed. That's real fluency.

skills.item_template: A single multiplication or division fact within 12 x 12. Numeric response, no context, no choices — speed and accuracy only.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common slips: 48 (6x8) or 36 (6x6)

vocabulary.definition: The answer you get when you multiply two numbers.
The answer you get when you divide one number by another.

next_steps.if_fail: Drill fact families daily with flash cards or a fact app; retest with a 1-minute sprint before moving on.

worked_example_script.text: Before answering 7 x 6 cold: what friendly fact is nearby? Most students know 7 x 5 = 35 -- so 7 x 6 is that plus one more 7. Rebuild it, don't guess it.
Write on the board: 7 x 6 = ___
What is 7 x 6? Say it as fast as you can.
If the answer comes in under 3 seconds, move on. If the student counts on fingers or stalls, don't give the answer — ask the next question.
What's a 7 fact you DO know for sure? Most students know 7 x 5 = 35.
If 7 x 5 = 35, how do you get to 7 x 6 from there?
One more group of 7: 35 + 7 = 42. Building from a known fact beats guessing every time.
Now write: 42 / 7 = ___. Same family, opposite direction.
How does knowing 7 x 6 = 42 make 42 / 7 free? What about 42 / 6?

skills.name: Understand a 'per' rate as a repeated equal amount

prerequisite_skill.description: Interpret multiplication as equal groups ('3 boxes with 5 in each box')
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Stickers come 4 to a pack. How many stickers are in 3 packs?

skills.i_do_script: The word 'per' is the engine of this whole standard. '$3 per cup' means EVERY cup adds another $3 — one cup costs 3, two cups cost 6, three cups cost 9. Watch me: 4 cups at $3 per cup is 4 groups of 3, so 4 x 3 = $12. If a student hears '$3 per cup' and thinks the whole order costs $3, everything after this breaks.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats the 'per' amount as a one-time total instead of an amount that repeats for every unit
canonical_error.example: For 'granola bars cost $2 each — what do 5 bars cost?' the student answers $2, or adds 2 + 5 = 7 instead of multiplying 2 x 5 = 10
canonical_error.why: The student reads '$2' as the price of the whole purchase, not the price of ONE unit. They haven't internalized that 'per' and 'each' mean the amount happens again for every single unit, which is multiplication.

redirect_script.prompt: Draw one circle for every bar and write $2 inside each circle. Now count the money circle by circle: 2, 4, 6... What operation did your counting just do?
redirect_script.praise: You saw that the $2 happens for every single bar. That's exactly what 'per' means.

skills.item_template: A one-sentence rate statement ('costs $4 each', 'eats 6 ounces per day') plus a small whole-number count. Student finds the total. Numeric response, no choices.

sample_items.stem: Pencils cost $2 each. What do 6 pencils cost?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 8 (adds 2 + 6) or 2 (treats $2 as the total) signal the 'per' gap

sample_items.stem: A dog eats 3 cups of food per day. How much in 5 days?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 8 (adds 3 + 5) or 3 (one-time reading of the rate)

sample_items.stem: Tickets cost $8 each. What do 4 tickets cost?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12 (adds 8 + 4) signals additive misreading of 'each'

sample_items.stem: A car goes 9 miles per gallon. How far on 6 gallons?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 15 (adds) or 9 (rate read as the total distance)

sample_items.stem: Erasers come 5 to a pack. How many in 7 packs?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12 (adds 5 + 7) signals equal-groups gap

sample_items.stem: A plant grows 2 inches per week. How much in 8 weeks?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 10 (adds 2 + 8) or 2 (one-time reading)

sample_items.stem: Juice boxes cost $1 each. What do 9 boxes cost?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 10 (adds 1 + 9); the rate of 1 exposes students who add instead of multiply

sample_items.stem: A baker uses 4 eggs per cake. How many eggs for 6 cakes?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 10 (adds 4 + 6) or 4 (rate read as total)

sample_items.stem: A bus travels 30 miles per hour. How far in 3 hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 33 (adds 30 + 3) or 30 (rate read as total)

sample_items.stem: Socks cost $6 per pair. What do 5 pairs cost?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 11 (adds 6 + 5) or 6 (one-time reading of the rate)

vocabulary.definition: An amount that happens for every one unit, like $3 per cup or 6 ounces per day.
A word that means 'for each one' — the amount repeats for every single unit.
Groups that all have the same amount in them; multiplying counts them all at once.

next_steps.if_fail: Model rates with counters — one pile per unit, the rate amount in each pile — until the student multiplies without prompting.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Granola bars cost $2 each. What do 5 bars cost?'
Before any math — what does 'each' mean in this sentence? Who pays $2: the whole order, or every single bar?
If the student says 'the order costs $2' or wants to add 2 + 5, they're reading the rate as a one-time amount. Don't correct yet — build it out.
Draw 5 boxes in a row. Write $2 inside the first box.
Does the second bar also cost $2? The third? Fill in every box.
Count the money box by box out loud. What are you counting by? 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
Counting by 2s five times — what operation is that? Write it as one multiplication.
Exactly — 5 x 2 = $10. 'Per' and 'each' always mean the amount repeats for every unit, and repeating equal amounts is multiplication. That idea powers everything we do next.

skills.name: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a real-world situation

prerequisite_skill.description: Understand that a letter can stand for a quantity in a situation
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In 'Mia sold c cups of lemonade,' what does c stand for?

skills.i_do_script: Every proportional situation has two quantities, and one of them drives the other. Watch me with 'the number of hours Maya babysits and the money she earns.' I ask: which one causes the other? Working more hours CAUSES more money — so hours is the independent variable (the input you choose) and money is the dependent variable (the output that depends on it). The test question is always 'which one depends on the other?'

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the two variables — names the input as dependent and the output as independent
canonical_error.example: For 'the number of cups sold determines the money earned,' the student says the number of cups is the dependent variable
canonical_error.why: The student picks whichever quantity is mentioned first or feels more important, instead of asking the cause-and-effect question. 'Independent' and 'dependent' are abstract labels until they're anchored to 'which one do you control?' and 'which one responds?'

redirect_script.stop: Hold on — let's ask the depends question.
redirect_script.prompt: Say this sentence both ways and pick the one that's true: 'The money earned depends on the cups sold' or 'The cups sold depend on the money earned.' Circle the quantity that DEPENDS — that's your dependent variable.
redirect_script.praise: You used the depends test instead of guessing. That works on every problem.

skills.item_template: A one- or two-sentence real-world statement naming two related quantities (often with letters). Student identifies the independent or dependent variable. MC with the two quantities plus 'both'/'neither' foils, or short constructed response with reasoning. DOK 1-3, easy — no calculation.

sample_items.stem:
The more miles, m, a person bikes, the more calories, c, they burn.

What is the dependent variable?
sample_items.answer: the number of calories burned
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choosing miles biked signals the swap error — the student picked the input. 'Both/neither' catch students with no cause-and-effect test at all.

sample_items.stem:
A cat eats the same amount of food each day. The number of days, d, determines the total ounces of food, f, the cat has eaten.

What is the independent variable?
sample_items.answer: the number of days
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choosing ounces of food is the swap error. 'The cat' catches students who name the actor in the story instead of a quantity.

sample_items.stem: Every week a painter is paid d dollars for working h hours. What is the dependent variable in this situation? Explain your reasoning.
sample_items.answer: The pay, d dollars, is the dependent variable because the amount of money depends on the number of hours worked. As hours increase, pay increases.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who answer 'hours' are swapping; students who can name d but not explain are pattern-matching on word order rather than using the depends test.

sample_items.stem:
A young man sells lemonade. The number of cups, c, he sells determines how much money, m, he earns.

What is the dependent variable?
sample_items.answer: the amount of money earned
sample_items.distractor_logic: Cups sold is the swap error; 'the young man' catches label-thinkers who name the person instead of a quantity.

sample_items.stem:
The number of gallons of gas, g, a car uses determines the number of miles, m, it can drive.

What is the independent variable?
sample_items.answer: the number of gallons of gas
choices: the number of gallons of gas
sample_items.distractor_logic: Miles driven is the swap error — it's the output. Students often pick it because the question 'feels like' it's about driving.

vocabulary.definition: A letter that stands for a quantity that can change, like h for hours.
The input — the quantity you choose or control, like the number of hours worked.
The output — the quantity that responds, like the money earned. It depends on the independent variable.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'The number of cups of lemonade, c, a boy sells determines how much money, m, he earns.'
There are two quantities in this story. What are they? Name both.
Here's the big question: which one causes the other? Does selling cups cause the money, or does the money cause the cups?
Selling cups causes the money. We call the cause the INDEPENDENT variable — it's the input, the thing that happens first. The money is the DEPENDENT variable — it depends on the cups.
Write the depends test on the board: '___ depends on ___.' Fill it in: 'The money earned depends on the cups sold.'
Try the sentence backwards: 'The cups sold depend on the money earned.' Does that make sense? Why not?
If the student says the backwards sentence sounds fine, ask: 'Can he sell more cups by wishing for more money, or does he get more money by selling more cups?' Force the cause-and-effect order.
Your turn: 'The number of hours worked, h, determines the pay, p.' Say the depends sentence and name both variables.

practice_problems.stem: The number of hours, h, Maria works determines her pay, p. Which quantity depends on the other?
practice_problems.answer: The pay depends on the hours worked.

practice_problems.stem: The more laps, l, a swimmer swims, the more calories, c, she burns. Name the two quantities in this situation.
practice_problems.answer: The number of laps swum and the number of calories burned.

practice_problems.stem: The number of tickets, t, a family buys determines the total cost, c. What is the independent variable and what is the dependent variable?
practice_problems.answer: Independent: the number of tickets. Dependent: the total cost.
practice_problems.notes: Watch for the swap — students who answer cost first without the depends test.

practice_problems.stem: A printer prints the same number of pages every minute. Let m be the minutes and p be the pages printed. Which variable is dependent? Say the depends sentence.
practice_problems.answer: p is dependent: the pages printed depend on the minutes of printing.
practice_problems.notes: The letters come in a tempting alphabetical order — the depends test has to beat word order.

practice_problems.stem: A student read: 'The number of bracelets, b, Keisha makes determines how much ribbon, r, she uses.' Find the error in the student's work and fix it.
shown_work: Student wrote: The independent variable is the ribbon used, r.
Student wrote: The dependent variable is the bracelets made, b.
practice_problems.answer: The labels are swapped. Making bracelets causes ribbon to be used, so b (bracelets) is independent and r (ribbon used) is dependent — the ribbon used depends on the bracelets made.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait of the canonical swap error.

practice_problems.stem: The number of days, d, a family camps determines the campground fee, f, they pay. What is the dependent variable?
practice_problems.answer: The fee, f — it depends on the number of days.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own real-world situation with two quantities where one depends on the other. Label the independent and dependent variables with letters.
practice_problems.answer: Any cause-and-effect pair, e.g., 'The number of songs, s, downloaded determines the total cost, c. Independent: s. Dependent: c.'
practice_problems.notes: Producing a situation is a deeper check than sorting someone else's.

practice_problems.stem: In 'the number of gallons of paint, g, determines the wall area, a, covered' — could a person argue the variables the other way? Explain why the given sentence fixes which one is independent.
practice_problems.answer: The word 'determines' fixes the direction: gallons is the cause (independent) and area covered is the effect (dependent). You buy paint first; the coverage responds.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-why stretch — pushes past pattern matching.

activities.title: Cause or Effect?
materials: Two header cards: 'Independent (the cause / input)' and 'Dependent (the effect / output)'
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the cards. Each card names one quantity from a two-quantity story printed at the top of the card.
2. Partners sort each card under Independent or Dependent, saying the depends sentence out loud each time: '___ depends on ___.'
3. Swap piles and check each other.
4. Debrief: which card was hardest, and what question settled it?

cards.text: Cups of lemonade sold (story: cups determine money)
Days of camping (story: days determine total fee)
Total campground fee (story: days determine total fee)
Gallons of gas used (story: gallons determine miles)

activities.title: The Swapped Labels
activities.instructions:
1. Students read the flawed work and say the depends sentence both directions.
2. They name which direction is true and relabel both variables.
3. Exit question: what one question do you ask yourself to tell independent from dependent?

content.worked_problem: Story: 'The number of bracelets, b, Keisha makes determines how much ribbon, r, she uses.' A student labeled r as independent and b as dependent.
content.error_step: The student swapped the labels — they made the output (ribbon used) the input.
content.why: The student didn't run the depends test. Making bracelets is the action Keisha controls; the ribbon used responds to it, so ribbon is dependent.

activities.title: Depends-On Duel
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a story strip (e.g., 'minutes of charging and phone battery percent') and read it aloud.
2. On a signal, every player writes I = ___ and D = ___ on their whiteboard.
3. Boards up together. One point for each correct label, plus a bonus point for saying a correct depends sentence.
4. Debrief: collect the sentences that started with 'depends on' — that phrase is the whole skill.

strategy_links.why: Which quantity causes the other is a genuine argument — think-pair-share forces students to defend the direction out loud.
The depends sentence frame ('___ depends on ___') is perfect for choral response until the test question is automatic.
Swapped labels are the one big error here — find-and-fix slips make the swap visible fast.

questioning_prompts: Which of these two quantities do you get to choose or control?
Say the sentence '___ depends on ___' both ways. Which way is actually true?
If the independent variable got bigger, what would happen to the other quantity?
The story names a person and two amounts. Which two things are the variables — and why isn't the person one of them?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the labels — calls the input dependent and the output independent.
misconception_redirects.say: Say this sentence both ways and pick the one that's true: 'The money earned depends on the cups sold' or 'The cups sold depend on the money earned.' Circle the quantity that DEPENDS — that's your dependent variable.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the depends test instead of guessing. That works on every problem.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student names the person or object in the story ('the painter', 'the cat') as a variable.
misconception_redirects.say: A variable is a quantity — a number that can change. The painter doesn't change; the HOURS and the DOLLARS do. Reread the story and underline the two amounts that can go up or down.
misconception_redirects.praise: Yes — you found the two quantities. Variables are always amounts, never people or things.

quick_checks.prompt: In 'the number of hours, h, determines the pay, d,' point to the dependent variable and say the depends sentence.
quick_checks.look_for: Points to d and says 'the pay depends on the hours.' Pointing to h means the swap error; naming 'the painter' means they haven't separated quantities from labels.

quick_checks.prompt: Give me a real-life pair where one amount depends on the other — you invent it.
quick_checks.look_for: A believable cause-and-effect pair with the direction stated correctly. A reversible or vague pair ('height and age of a rock') signals the depends test isn't anchored yet.

worked_solution.stem: The number of cups of lemonade, c, a boy sells determines how much money, m, he earns. Identify the independent and dependent variables.
worked_solution.answer: Independent: c, the number of cups sold. Dependent: m, the money earned.

steps.math: Two quantities: cups sold (c) and money earned (m)
steps.annotation: First find the two amounts that can change. The boy himself is not a variable — only the amounts are.

steps.math: Depends test: 'The money earned depends on the cups sold.'
steps.annotation: Say the sentence both directions. Only one direction is true — money responds to cups, not the other way around.
The cause is independent; the quantity that depends is dependent. Label both.

faded_example.stem: The number of days, d, a family rents a kayak determines the total cost, t. Identify the independent and dependent variables.
faded_example.answer: Independent: d, the number of days. Dependent: t, the total cost.

steps.math: Two quantities: days rented (d) and total cost (t)
steps.annotation: Underline the two amounts that can change.
Say the depends sentence in the direction that's true: '___ depends on ___.'
Label the cause as independent and the responder as dependent.

sentence_starters: ___ depends on ___, so ___ is the dependent variable.
I control ___, so it is the independent variable.

skills.name: Complete a table of values for a proportional relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply whole numbers and simple decimals by a one-digit number

skills.i_do_script: A proportional table is a rate written down the page: every y-value is the SAME multiplier times its x-value. Watch me with 'a cat eats 7 ounces per day': day 1 is 7, day 2 is 14, day 3 is 21. To find the missing value at day 4, I don't count down the column — I multiply across the row: 7 x 4 = 28. Multiply across, don't crawl down.

canonical_error.pattern: Extends the table by adding down the y-column instead of multiplying across the row, which breaks whenever the x-values skip
canonical_error.example: For a $6-per-ticket table with rows x = 1, 2, 3, 5, the student fills the x = 5 row with 24 (18 + 6, just adding one more 6) instead of 30 (6 x 5)
canonical_error.why: In a table with consecutive x-values, adding the rate down the column happens to work, so the student learns 'add the same number each row' instead of 'multiply x by the rate.' The moment a row is skipped, the shortcut silently fails.

redirect_script.prompt: Put your finger on the x-value in the row you're filling. Now multiply THAT number by the rate: rate times x. Does your answer come from the row you're in, or from the row above it?
redirect_script.praise: You multiplied across the row instead of counting down the column. That works even when the table skips.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate ('$1.50 per cup', '7 ounces per day') with a two-column table (x, y) that has one missing y-value, sometimes with skipped x-values. Student supplies the missing value. Numeric response with a data_table figure. Whole numbers for medium, decimals for difficult.

sample_items.stem:
A cat eats 7 ounces of food per day. The table shows the relationship between the number of days, d, and the total ounces of food, f.

What is the missing value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 35 comes from copying the next row's pattern wrong; 22 comes from adding 1 to 21 instead of multiplying 7 x 4.

sample_items.stem:
Carson sells lemonade for $1.50 per cup. The table shows the relationship between cups sold, c, and money earned, m.

What is the missing value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5.50 comes from adding 1 instead of 1.50 to the row above; 4.50 comes from copying the c = 3 row.

sample_items.stem:
A florist uses 12 flowers per bouquet. The table shows bouquets, b, and flowers, f. Notice the table skips from b = 3 to b = 6.

What is the missing value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 48 is the classic add-down error — adding one more 12 after b = 3 instead of multiplying 12 x 6.

sample_items.stem:
A recipe uses 0.5 cup of sugar per batch of cookies. The table shows batches, b, and cups of sugar, s.

What is the missing value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2.5 comes from copying the b = 5 pattern one row too early; 6.5 comes from adding 0.5 to the batch number instead of multiplying.

vocabulary.definition: A relationship where one quantity is always the same multiplier times the other.
The 'per one' amount — how much y grows for every single x.
A chart pairing each x-value with its y-value, one pair per row.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a two-column table on the board. Header: 'days (d)' and 'ounces of food (f)'. Fill in the rows (1, 7), (2, 14), (3, 21), then (4, blank), then (5, 35). Say: 'A cat eats 7 ounces of food per day.'
Look at the complete rows. What do you do to each d to get its f? Check every row before you answer.
Let's confirm the rate. Divide f by d in each complete row: 7/1, 14/2, 21/3. Do you get the same number every time? What is the rate?
Now look at the blank row. What number is in the d-column?

Watch the METHOD, not just the number. The classic error here is crawling DOWN the column — adding one more 7 to the 21 above — instead of multiplying across the row. Because the days don't skip, crawling lands on 28 and looks fine, but that habit breaks the moment a table jumps a day. Make the student say whether they multiplied 7 x 4 or just added 7 to 21.
The row says d = 4. If the cat eats 7 ounces every day for 4 days, how many ounces is that in total? Multiply across the row.
7 x 4 = 28. Multiply ACROSS the row — the rate times the d-value in THIS row. That is why the method still works even when a table skips.
Prove it beats crawling: if I added a row for d = 10, what would f be? You can't get there by adding one 7 at a time — so multiply, 7 x 10 = 70.

practice_problems.stem: A hen lays 1 egg per day. Fill in the missing value: 5 days, ___ eggs.
Stickers cost $2 each. Complete the pair: 6 stickers, $___.
A pool fills at 8 gallons per minute. The table pairs minutes, m, with gallons, g. Fill in the missing value.
practice_problems.notes: The table skips m = 5 and m = 6 — add-down students will write 40.

practice_problems.stem: Tickets cost $9 each. The table pairs tickets, t, with cost, c. Fill in the missing value.
A car wash charges $8 per car. The table pairs cars, c, with dollars, d: rows are (1, 8), (2, 16), (3, 24), (7, ?). Devon filled in the missing value. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Devon added one more 8 down the column, but the table jumps from c = 3 to c = 7. Multiply across the row: 8 x 7 = 56.
practice_problems.notes: Fresh-number bait of the canonical add-down error.

practice_problems.stem: A runner burns 100 calories per mile. The table pairs miles, m, with calories, c. Fill in the missing value.
Ribbon costs $1.25 per foot. Complete the table pair for 8 feet.
practice_problems.notes: Decimal rate — spec's 'difficult' tier.

practice_problems.stem: Build your own proportional table: pick a rate, make 4 rows, and skip at least one x-value. Trade with a partner and fill in each other's missing value.
practice_problems.answer: Any table where every y equals the chosen rate times its x, with a skipped x-value.
practice_problems.notes: Producing the trap is the strongest proof they understand it.

activities.title: Build the Table with Cups
materials: Blank two-column table on a whiteboard
activities.instructions:
1. Pose: 'Lemonade costs $3 per cup.' Each cup gets 3 counters.
2. Students line up 1 cup, then 2, then 3, recording (cups, total counters) as table rows.
3. Now say: 'Jump to 7 cups WITHOUT building 4, 5, and 6.' Groups must find the total with one multiplication and then verify by building it.
4. Debrief: why did 3 x 7 beat counting up? What if the order were 100 cups?

activities.title: The Skipped-Row Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs check every row of Devon's table with multiplication: rate times x.
2. They circle the row where his answer breaks and write the fix.
3. Exit question: what should you look at FIRST before filling any missing table value?

content.worked_problem: Car wash: $8 per car. Table rows (1, 8), (2, 16), (3, 24), (7, ?). Devon wrote 24 + 8 = 32.
content.error_step: Devon added the rate once to the previous row instead of multiplying the rate by the x-value in his own row.
content.why: Adding down the column only works when x goes up by 1 each row. The table skips from 3 to 7, so the correct value is 8 x 7 = 56.

activities.title: Match the Row to Its Value
activities.instructions:
1. Each left card names a rate and an x-value; each right card is a y-value.
2. Partners match every row to its value by multiplying, saying the equation out loud ('4 x 6 = 24').
3. Two decoy values are add-down traps — the debrief names why they tempt people.

strategy_links.why: Cups-and-counters make 'the rate rides with every x' concrete before the table abstracts it.
The add-down error is invisible until a skipped row exposes it — find-and-fix work makes the trap explicit.
Whiteboard pass on table rows lets the teacher spot column-crawlers in real time across the group.

questioning_prompts: Before you fill the blank — what x-value is in YOUR row?
What one multiplication takes you from any x in this table straight to its y?
The table skips some x-values. Does your method still work? How do you know?
What would the y-value be for x = 0? What does that mean in the story?
If I gave you x = 100, could you find y without filling in 99 rows? Show me.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student fills a missing value by adding the rate to the row above, even when the x-values skip.
misconception_redirects.say: Put your finger on the x-value in the row you're filling. Now multiply THAT number by the rate: rate times x. Does your answer come from the row you're in, or from the row above it?
misconception_redirects.praise: You multiplied across the row instead of counting down the column. That works even when the table skips.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds the rate from one row but then uses a different multiplier on the next row (rate drifts).
misconception_redirects.say: In a proportional table the multiplier NEVER changes. Check it on every complete row: divide y by x each time. Do you get the same number in every row?
misconception_redirects.praise: You verified the rate on every row before using it. That's exactly how you catch a fake proportional table.

quick_checks.prompt: Table: (1, 6), (2, 12), (5, ?). Fill the blank and tell me how.
quick_checks.look_for: 30 via 6 x 5. An answer of 18 means add-down thinking — the student added one more 6 after row 2.

quick_checks.prompt: What is the rate in the table (2, 10), (4, 20), (6, 30)? How do you know?
quick_checks.look_for: 5, found by dividing y by x in any row. A student who says 10 (the difference between y-values) is reading down the column, not across the row.

worked_solution.stem: A florist uses 12 flowers per bouquet. The table pairs bouquets, b, with flowers, f: (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), (6, ?). Find the missing value.

steps.annotation: Every complete row has the same multiplier — divide f by b to confirm the rate is 12.

steps.math: The blank row has b = 6, not b = 4
steps.annotation: Look at the x-column first. The table skips — so adding one more 12 to 36 would be wrong.
Multiply across the row: the rate times the x-value in this row. 72 flowers.

faded_example.stem: A pool fills at 8 gallons per minute. The table pairs minutes, m, with gallons, g: (1, 8), (2, 16), (3, 24), (7, ?). Find the missing value.

steps.annotation: Confirm the same multiplier works on every complete row.
Look at the x-column in the blank row. What number is there? (Careful — the table skips.)
Multiply the rate by that x-value to fill the blank.

sentence_starters: Every y in this table is ___ times its x, so the rate is ___.
My row has x = ___, so I multiply ___ x ___ instead of adding down.

skills.name: Write the equation y = px that matches a proportional table

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the constant rate in a proportional table (skill 6RP5-S2)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: In the table (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15), what is one y divided by its x?

skills.i_do_script: Once a table shows the same multiplier in every row, we can write the whole table as one equation: y = px, where p is the rate. Watch me with the table (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12): I divide y by x in any row — 8 divided by 2 is 4 — so the equation is y = 4x. The order of that division matters: it's always y DIVIDED BY x, the dependent over the independent. Then I test it: does 4 x 3 give 12? Yes. The equation is the table, compressed into one line.

canonical_error.pattern: Inverts the rate — divides x by y instead of y by x, producing y = x/p when the table shows y = px
canonical_error.example: For the table (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12), the student computes 2/8 and writes y = x/4 instead of y = 4x
canonical_error.why: The student knows the rate comes from dividing the two columns but doesn't track WHICH column goes on top. Division isn't commutative, so y/x and x/y give reciprocal rates — and the inverted equation y = x/4 even 'looks right' because it contains the same numbers.

redirect_script.stop: Stop — test your equation on a row.
redirect_script.prompt: Pick any complete row from the table and plug its x into your equation. Does the equation spit out that row's y? If not, you divided in the wrong order — the rate is y divided by x, dependent over independent.
redirect_script.praise: You tested your equation against a real row. An equation that survives the row test is right.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate context with a completed two-column table (data_table figure). Student selects or writes the equation expressing the dependent variable in terms of the independent variable, in the form y = px. MC distractors: the inverted rate y = x/p, the additive y = p + x, and an off-by-one rate.

sample_items.stem:
A bakery uses 5 cups of flour per loaf of bread. The table shows the relationship between loaves, x, and cups of flour, y.

Which equation represents this relationship?
sample_items.answer: y = 5x
sample_items.distractor_logic: y = x/5 is the k-inversion (divided x by y); y = 5 + x is additive thinking; y = 6x comes from misreading a row.

sample_items.stem:
A mowing company must hire 1 employee for every 7 yards it mows. The table shows yards mowed, y, and employees hired, e.

Which equation represents e, the number of employees hired for y yards?
sample_items.answer: e = y/7
sample_items.distractor_logic: e = 7y is the inversion in the other direction — students who always multiply attach the 7 to the wrong side. Testing a row (14 yards, 2 employees) settles it: 14/7 = 2.

sample_items.stem:
An employee earns the same amount each hour. The table shows hours worked, h, and money earned, m.

Which equation represents this relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: m = h/3.50 is the inversion; m = 3.50 + h is additive; m = 7h comes from using the h = 2 row's m-value as the rate.

sample_items.stem: A cat eats the same amount of food each day. The table shows days, d, and total ounces eaten, f. Write an equation that expresses f in terms of d.
sample_items.answer: f = 9d
sample_items.distractor_logic: f = d/9 signals the inversion; d = 9f signals swapped dependent/independent. Both fail the row test on (2, 18).

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence with an equals sign that says two amounts are the same.
A relationship you can write as y = px — y is always p times x.
The input, x — the equation is written with y alone on one side and x on the other.
The output, y — the quantity the equation expresses in terms of x.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the table: x-column 1, 2, 3, 4 and y-column 5, 10, 15, 20. Say: 'A bakery uses the same amount of flour in every loaf — x is loaves, y is cups of flour. Write ONE equation for this whole table.'
We want a single equation that stands for every row. In each row, what is y doing to x?
To find the rate from a row, which number gets divided by which? Try the second row: is it 10 divided by 2, or 2 divided by 10?
This is the inversion moment. If the student divides 2 by 10, or shrugs, don't correct — let them compute both 10/2 = 5 and 2/10 = 0.2 and hold on to both for the test step.
The rate is y divided by x — dependent over independent. 10/2 = 5, and 15/3 = 5 too. So my claim is y = 5x.
Let's test the claim on a row we didn't use to find the rate. Row (4, 20): does 5 x 4 give 20? Now test the wrong-order version, y = x/5: does 4/5 give 20?
5 x 4 = 20 matches the table; 4/5 does not. The row test kills the inverted equation instantly, so our equation is y = 5x.
Your turn: table (1, 6), (2, 12), (5, 30). Write the equation AND show me your row test.

practice_problems.stem: In the table (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), what is the rate — the number every x is multiplied by?
A table shows y = 8 when x = 1, and y = 16 when x = 2. Fill in the blank: y = ___ x.
practice_problems.answer: y = 8x

practice_problems.stem: Movie tickets cost the same amount each. The table pairs tickets, x, with dollars, y. Write the equation.
practice_problems.answer: y = 11x
practice_problems.notes: Ask for the row test out loud: 11 x 3 = 33.

practice_problems.stem: A table pairs hours, x, with miles, y: (1, 6), (2, 12), (4, 24). Jayla wrote an equation. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Jayla divided x by y instead of y by x, so her rate is flipped. The rate is 12/2 = 6, and the equation is y = 6x. The row test proves it: her equation gives y = 4/6 for x = 4, but the table says 24; y = 6x gives 6 x 4 = 24.
practice_problems.notes: The k-inversion bait — the canonical error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: The table pairs pounds of apples, x, with cost in dollars, y: (2, 5), (4, 10), (6, 15). Write the equation.
practice_problems.notes: Rate isn't visible in a (1, ?) row — students must divide 5/2. Watch for y = 2x from eyeballing.

practice_problems.stem: Which equation matches the table (1, 4), (3, 12), (5, 20): y = 4x or y = x/4? Prove your choice with the row test on (3, 12).
practice_problems.answer: y = 4x. Row test: 4 x 3 = 12 matches the table; 3/4 does not.
practice_problems.notes: Forces the direct comparison between the correct equation and the inverted one.

practice_problems.stem: A table pairs gallons, x, with miles, y, and its equation is y = 28x. Write ONE new row that could appear in the table, and one row that could NOT.
practice_problems.answer: Could: any (x, 28x) pair, e.g., (3, 84). Could not: any pair where y is not 28 times x, e.g., (2, 30).
practice_problems.notes: Reverses direction — from equation back to table rows.

practice_problems.stem: The table pairs yards mowed, y, with employees, e: (8, 1), (16, 2), (24, 3). Write the equation for e in terms of y, and explain why the rate is a fraction.
practice_problems.answer: e = y/8 (or e = (1/8)y). Each employee covers 8 yards, so the number of employees is the yards divided by 8 — the rate is 1/8 because e grows by 1 for every 8 yards.
practice_problems.notes: The legitimate divide-direction case — distinguishes real understanding from 'always multiply.'

activities.title: Table Meets Equation
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the table cards and equation cards face up.
2. Partners match each table to its equation — but every match must be defended with a row test said out loud ('6 times 2 is 12 — it survives').
3. Two decoy equations are inverted rates; the debrief asks why those decoys are so tempting.

activities.title: The Flipped Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Students run the row test on Jayla's equation using two different table rows.
2. They name exactly which division she did backwards and write the corrected equation.
3. Exit question: which variable goes on TOP when you compute the rate, and how do you remember?

content.worked_problem: Table: hours x and miles y — (1, 6), (2, 12), (4, 24). Jayla computed 2/12 = 1/6 and wrote y = x/6.
content.error_step: Jayla divided the independent variable by the dependent variable — x over y instead of y over x.
content.why: The rate in y = px is y divided by x (12/2 = 6), so the equation is y = 6x. Her flipped rate fails the row test: for x = 4 her equation predicts 4/6, not 24.

activities.title: Equation Survivor
activities.instructions:
1. Project a proportional table. Every player secretly writes an equation candidate.
2. Reveal boards. The group tests every candidate against one table row — equations that fail are 'voted off.'
3. Rotate who picks the test row. Inverted-rate equations get eliminated publicly, which is the point.
4. Debrief: what kinds of wrong equations kept showing up, and what row test caught them fastest?

strategy_links.why: Pairing a correct y = px derivation with the inverted y = x/p right next to it makes the division-order error unmissable.
The flipped rate is this skill's signature bug — find-and-fix items train the row test as the repair tool.
'Which number goes on top?' is a real debate — partners defending y/x versus x/y surfaces the reasoning.

questioning_prompts: What is the rate in this table, and exactly which division did you do to get it?
Test your equation on a row you haven't used yet. Does it survive?
Why does y = 4x and y = x/4 contain the same numbers but mean different things?
Which variable is dependent here — and which side of the equation should it sit on alone?
If the table had a row (1, ?), what would the y-value be, and how does that connect to p?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes y = x/p when the table shows y = px — they divided x by y to find the rate.
misconception_redirects.say: Pick any complete row from the table and plug its x into your equation. Does the equation spit out that row's y? If not, you divided in the wrong order — the rate is y divided by x, dependent over independent.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested your equation against a real row. An equation that survives the row test is right.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes an additive equation like y = 5 + x because the first row is (1, 6) or the numbers 'fit once.'
misconception_redirects.say: An equation that only works on one row is a coincidence, not a rule. Test y = 5 + x on the second row. Then test y = 6x. Which one survives every row?
misconception_redirects.praise: You made the equation survive the whole table, not just one lucky row.

quick_checks.prompt: Table: (1, 7), (2, 14), (3, 21). Write the equation in 15 seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: y = 7x. Writing y = x/7 is the inversion; y = 7 + x means additive thinking — both need the row test reteach.

quick_checks.prompt: Your friend wrote y = x/3 for the table (1, 3), (2, 6). Convince me in one sentence they're wrong.
quick_checks.look_for: A row test: 'plug in x = 2 — her equation gives 2/3, but the table says 6; it should be y = 3x.' Restating the rule without testing a row is weaker evidence.

worked_solution.stem: A bakery uses the same amount of flour per loaf. The table pairs loaves, x, with cups of flour, y: (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15), (4, 20). Write the equation.

steps.annotation: Divide dependent by independent — y on top. Check another row: 15/3 = 5. Same rate, good.
A proportional relationship always writes as y = px. Drop the rate in for p.

steps.math: Row test: x = 4 gives y = 5 x 4 = 20
steps.annotation: The table's row (4, 20) matches. The inverted equation y = x/5 would give 4/5 — the test rejects it.

faded_example.stem: The table pairs hours, x, with pages read, y: (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36). Write the equation.

steps.annotation: Dependent over independent — y goes on top.
Write the equation in the form y = px using your rate.
Prove it with a row test on (3, 36).

sentence_starters: The rate is ___ because y divided by x is ___ in every row.
My equation survives the row test: when x = ___, it gives ___, which matches the table.

skills.name: Write an equation from a real-world situation and use it to solve

prerequisite_skill.description: Write y = px from a completed table (skill 6RP5-S3)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: The table (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12) — what equation matches it?

skills.i_do_script: Now we skip the table and write the equation straight from the story. Watch me with 'Leah earns $9 per dog walk': first I name the variables — w is the walks (independent, she controls it) and m is the money (dependent). The 'per' amount is my rate, so m = 9w. Then the equation does the work: for 12 walks, m = 9 x 12 = 108 dollars. Name the variables, put the rate with the independent one, then let the equation answer the question.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the equation solved for the wrong variable — attaches the rate to the dependent variable, e.g. h = 8m instead of m = 8h
canonical_error.example: For 'Marcus earns $8 per hour; write money m in terms of hours h,' the student writes h = 8m — which secretly says the money gets multiplied by 8 to make hours
canonical_error.why: The student treats the two letters as interchangeable slots and puts the rate next to whichever letter comes first. They haven't connected 'express the dependent in terms of the independent' to a structure: the dependent variable sits ALONE on the left, and the rate multiplies the independent variable. h = 8m is the same inversion as y = x/8 in disguise.

redirect_script.stop: Wait — which variable should be alone?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask the story: which amount is the answer you want (dependent)? That letter sits alone on the left. The rate multiplies the OTHER letter. Now test with one easy number: 1 hour should earn $8 — does your equation say that?
redirect_script.praise: You tested your equation with an easy value before trusting it. That habit catches every flipped equation.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate statement. Part A: write the equation in the form y = px expressing the dependent variable in terms of the independent. Part B: use the equation to find the dependent value for a given independent value. Whole numbers for medium, decimals for difficult.

sample_items.stem:
Leah walks dogs and earns $9 per walk.

Part A: Write an equation for the money she earns, m, in terms of the number of walks, w.
Part B: Use your equation to find how much she earns for 12 walks.
sample_items.answer: Part A: m = 9w; Part B: m = 9 x 12 = 108 dollars
sample_items.distractor_logic: w = 9m is the flipped equation; Part B answers of 21 (9 + 12) signal additive thinking.

sample_items.stem:
A machine fills 15 bottles per minute.

Part A: Write an equation for the number of bottles filled, b, in terms of minutes, m.
Part B: How many bottles does the machine fill in 8 minutes?
sample_items.answer: Part A: b = 15m; Part B: b = 15 x 8 = 120 bottles
sample_items.distractor_logic: m = 15b flips the equation; 23 (15 + 8) is the additive slip.

sample_items.stem: A person pays a dog-walking service $9 for each week of walks. Which equation represents the relationship between the number of weeks, w, and the total money paid, d?
sample_items.answer: d = 9w
sample_items.distractor_logic: w = 9d attaches the rate to the wrong variable (the flip); d = w/9 is the k-inversion; d = 9 + w is additive.

sample_items.stem:
Gas costs $3.25 per gallon.

Part A: Write an equation for the total cost, c, in terms of gallons, g.
Part B: Find the cost of 10 gallons.
sample_items.answer: Part A: c = 3.25g; Part B: c = 3.25 x 10 = 32.50 dollars
sample_items.distractor_logic: g = 3.25c is the flip; 13.25 (3.25 + 10) is additive; 3.25 alone means the rate was read as a total.

vocabulary.definition: A letter standing for a quantity in the story, like w for walks.
The output — in y = px it sits alone on the left side of the equation.
The input — in y = px it is the letter the rate multiplies.
A relationship of the form y = px: the output is always the rate times the input.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Marcus earns $8 per hour at his job.' Underneath: 'Write an equation for his pay, m, in terms of hours worked, h. Then find his pay for 25 hours.'
First, the two variables. Which letter is the independent variable — the one Marcus controls — and which is the dependent one?
The dependent variable gets to sit alone on the left of the equals sign. Which letter sits alone?
Now the rate. The $8 happens for every WHAT? So which letter does the 8 multiply?
m = 8h. The pay, alone on the left, equals 8 times the hours. Read it back as a sentence: 'money is 8 dollars for every hour.' It matches the story.

If the student wrote h = 8m, don't just fix it — test it. Ask: 'Plug in 1 hour of work. Your equation says 1 = 8m, so m is 12.5 cents. Does Marcus earn 12.5 cents for an hour?' Let the absurd result do the teaching.
Now use the equation for 25 hours. What does m equal? Show the substitution.
Your turn: 'A printer prints 30 pages per minute.' Write the equation for pages p in terms of minutes t, then find p for 6 minutes.

practice_problems.stem: Apples cost $2 per pound. Write the equation for cost, c, in terms of pounds, p.
practice_problems.answer: c = 2p

practice_problems.stem: Using the equation m = 5h, find m when h = 4.
A bus travels 45 miles per hour. Write an equation for distance, d, in terms of hours, h, then find d for 6 hours.
practice_problems.answer: d = 45h; d = 45 x 6 = 270 miles
practice_problems.notes: Watch for h = 45d — the flipped equation.

practice_problems.stem: A florist uses 12 roses per centerpiece. The table shows the pattern. Write the equation for roses, r, in terms of centerpieces, c, then find r for 9 centerpieces.
practice_problems.answer: r = 12c; r = 12 x 9 = 108 roses
practice_problems.notes: Ratio table feeds the equation — the table is scaffolding, the equation answers the far-away value.

practice_problems.stem: 'A charity walk raises $6 for every mile, m, walked. Write an equation for the total raised, t.' Find the error in Ben's work and fix it.
shown_work: Ben's check: for 2 miles, m = 6t means 2 = 6t
practice_problems.answer: Ben flipped the equation — he attached the rate to the total instead of the miles. The total depends on the miles, so t sits alone: t = 6m. Check: 2 miles gives t = 6 x 2 = $12, which matches the story. Ben's version says 2 miles forces t to be 1/3 of a dollar, which is nonsense.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical flip error with fresh numbers — the k-inversion written as a variable swap.

practice_problems.stem: A faucet leaks 3 ounces of water per hour. Write the equation for ounces leaked, n, in terms of hours, h. How much leaks in 24 hours?
practice_problems.answer: n = 3h; n = 3 x 24 = 72 ounces

practice_problems.stem: Write a real-world situation that the equation p = 4s could represent. Say what p, 4, and s each mean, and which variable is dependent.
practice_problems.answer: Any 'per' story with rate 4, e.g., 'Each sandwich uses 4 pickle slices: s sandwiches use p = 4s slices.' p is dependent, s is independent, 4 is the rate.
practice_problems.notes: Equation-to-story reversal — the deepest check of ownership.

practice_problems.stem: Trail mix costs $4.50 per pound. Write the equation for cost c in terms of pounds p, then find the cost of 2.5 pounds.
practice_problems.notes: Decimal rate AND decimal input — the spec's difficult tier.

activities.title: Story, Equation, Check
activities.instructions:
1. Partners match each story card to its equation card.
2. Every match must pass the easy-number test out loud: plug in 1 unit and check the story ('1 hour should earn $8 — does it?').
3. Two decoys are flipped equations; the debrief names how the test exposed them.

pairs.left: Erin earns $8 per hour. (m = money, h = hours)
A recipe uses 3 eggs per cake. (e = eggs, c = cakes)
A train goes 50 miles each hour. (d = miles, h = hours)
Each table seats 6 guests. (g = guests, t = tables)

activities.title: The Backwards Equation
activities.instructions:
1. Students plug an easy value (2 miles) into Ben's equation and into their own fix, and compare which one matches the story.
2. They write one sentence naming what Ben attached to the wrong letter.
3. Exit question: which variable sits alone on the left, and how does the story tell you?

content.worked_problem: A charity walk raises $6 for every mile walked. Ben wrote m = 6t (m = miles, t = total dollars).
content.error_step: Ben put the rate with the dependent variable and left the independent variable alone — the equation is flipped.
content.why: The total depends on the miles, so t sits alone on the left: t = 6m. For 2 miles the correct equation gives $12; Ben's gives t = 1/3, which the story immediately contradicts.

activities.title: Rate Machine
materials: Index cards labeled INPUT and OUTPUT
activities.instructions:
1. One student is the Machine holding the rate card 'x 7.' Others feed INPUT cards (a number of hours) into the Machine.
2. The Machine multiplies and hands back the OUTPUT (pay).
3. After 4 rounds, the group writes the machine as an equation: output = 7 x input, then with letters: m = 7h.
4. Swap rate cards and repeat. Debrief: which letter does the rate always ride with — the input or the output?

strategy_links.why: Story-to-equation is a procedure students must own solo — I do / we do / you do fits the handoff exactly.
Thinking aloud 'which letter is dependent... which letter does the rate multiply...' models the internal checklist this skill needs.
The flipped equation (h = 8m) looks fine on paper — analyzing why it fails the easy-number test is the fastest cure.

questioning_prompts: Which amount is the answer the question wants? That's your dependent variable — where does it go in the equation?
The rate is 'per' WHAT? So which letter does it multiply?
Plug in 1 for the independent variable. Does your equation say what the story says?
Read your equation back as an English sentence. Does it tell the same story?
Could you have answered Part B without the equation? What does the equation buy you for x = 100?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the equation flipped — h = 8m for 'earns $8 per hour' — attaching the rate to the dependent variable.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask the story: which amount is the answer you want (dependent)? That letter sits alone on the left. The rate multiplies the OTHER letter. Now test with one easy number: 1 hour should earn $8 — does your equation say that?
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested your equation with an easy value before trusting it. That habit catches every flipped equation.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes y = p + x — adds the rate once instead of multiplying ('$8 per hour' becomes m = 8 + h).
misconception_redirects.say: Test 2 hours. Your equation says 8 + 2 = $10. Count it by hand: $8 for the first hour, $8 for the second — $16. The 8 happens EVERY hour, so it multiplies. What should the equation be?
misconception_redirects.praise: You caught it — a repeating amount multiplies the variable. Adding is for one-time amounts, and there are none here.

quick_checks.prompt: 'A candle burns 2 inches per hour.' Write the equation for inches burned, n, in terms of hours, h — 20 seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: n = 2h. h = 2n is the flip; n = 2 + h is additive. Either miss means run the easy-number test together.

quick_checks.prompt: Your equation is d = 55h. What is d when h = 4, and what do the 55 and the 4 mean in a story?
quick_checks.look_for: 220, with 55 as a rate ('55 miles each hour') and 4 as the input. Correct arithmetic with no story meaning signals symbol-pushing.

worked_solution.stem: Marcus earns $8 per hour. Write an equation for his pay, m, in terms of hours worked, h. Then find his pay for 25 hours.

steps.annotation: Name both variables first. Marcus controls the hours; the pay responds.
The dependent variable sits alone on the left. The rate multiplies the independent variable — $8 rides with every hour.
One hour should earn $8, and it does. The flipped equation h = 8m would say one hour earns 12.5 cents — rejected.
Now the equation does the work: 25 hours earns $200.

faded_example.stem: A printer prints 30 pages per minute. Write an equation for pages printed, p, in terms of minutes, t. Then find p for 6 minutes.

steps.annotation: Name the variables — the pages depend on the minutes.
Dependent alone on the left; the rate multiplies the independent variable.
Test it with an easy number: what should 1 minute print, and does your equation agree?
Substitute t = 6 and compute p.

sentence_starters: The ___ depends on the ___, so my equation starts '___ ='.
The rate ___ happens for every ___, so it multiplies ___.

skills.name: Graph a proportional relationship and connect it to the equation

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot ordered pairs in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (3, 5), which direction do you move first, and how far?

skills.i_do_script: A proportional relationship isn't just a table and an equation — it's also a picture. Watch me graph y = 3x: I turn table rows into ordered pairs — (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9) — always (x, y), independent first. I plot each pair: across 1, up 3. The points line up in a perfectly straight line, and that line passes through (0, 0), because zero of anything costs zero. Straight line through the origin — that's the signature of every y = px graph.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps the coordinates when plotting — writes or plots (y, x) instead of (x, y)
canonical_error.example: For y = 4x at x = 2, the student plots the point (8, 2) instead of (2, 8) — moving 8 across and 2 up
canonical_error.why: The student computed correctly but doesn't attach meaning to the order of an ordered pair. Since both numbers are 'the answer,' they list the bigger or more interesting number first. The convention — independent variable first, across before up — hasn't been anchored.

redirect_script.stop: Freeze — check the order of your pair.
redirect_script.prompt: An ordered pair is (across, up) — the independent variable always rides first. Say it as you plot: 'across 2, up 8.' Now check: does your point sit above the 2 on the x-axis?
redirect_script.praise: Across first, then up — you plotted the pair in the right order and the point landed on the line.

skills.item_template: A proportional context with an equation or short table. Student converts rows to ordered pairs, identifies which point is (or is not) on the graph, or explains the through-the-origin property. Coordinate_grid figure showing the line and/or plotted points. Never asks the student to derive the equation FROM the graph (out of scope for grade 6).

sample_items.stem: Bananas cost $2 per pound, so y = 2x gives the cost, y, of x pounds. Which ordered pair is on the graph of this relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (6, 3) is the swapped pair; (2, 1) is swapped AND inverted (x/2); (3, 5) is close-but-additive (3 + 2).

sample_items.stem: The table for f = 4d pairs days, d, with ounces of food, f: (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 12). Which ordered pair represents day 3 on the graph?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (12, 3) is the swap; (3, 4) pairs day 3 with day 1's value; (4, 12) misreads which column is which.

sample_items.stem: Every graph of a proportional relationship y = px passes through one special point. Which point is it?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (1, 1) is only on the graph when p = 1; (0, 1) and (1, 0) sit on an axis but not at the origin — students who memorized 'starts at the corner' loosely pick these.

sample_items.stem: Jon graphed the point (5, 15) for the equation y = 3x. Is his point on the line? Show how you know.
sample_items.answer: Yes. When x = 5, y = 3 x 5 = 15, so (5, 15) is on the line.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who can't verify are missing the equation-to-graph link; a 'no' answer often means they checked 5 x 15 or misread the pair order.

sample_items.stem: Amy earns $8 per hour, so her pay follows m = 8h. She plotted her pay for 2 hours at the point (16, 2). What did Amy do wrong, and what is the correct point?
sample_items.answer: She swapped the coordinates. The independent variable (hours) goes first: the correct point is (2, 16).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Direct bait of the coordinate-swap error; students who see nothing wrong plot pairs by size, not by role.

sample_items.stem: The graph shows y = 5x, where y is the total price in dollars of x notebooks. What is the y-value of the point on the line where x = 2?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7 (5 + 2) is additive; 2.5 signals reading the axes backwards (x/2).

sample_items.stem: Which of these points is NOT on the graph of y = 4x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Checking requires multiplying every pair: 4 x 4 = 16, not 20. Students who pick (5, 20) think a repeated y-value is suspicious; the rest are on the line.

sample_items.stem: The points (1, 3), (2, 6), and (3, 9) from a ratio table are plotted. If the pattern continues, what y-value pairs with x = 5?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 12 (adding 3 to 9 only once — the add-down error, since x skips from 3 to 5); 8 (adding 5 + 3).

sample_items.stem: Does the graph of y = 7x pass through the origin? Explain how the equation tells you.
sample_items.answer: Yes. When x = 0, y = 7 x 0 = 0, so the point (0, 0) is on the line. Zero items cost zero dollars.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who say 'no' or 'can't tell without the graph' haven't linked substitution to points; the equation itself answers it.

sample_items.stem: A drink machine pours 6 ounces per second, following n = 6t. List the ordered pairs for t = 1, 2, and 3, in correct order.
sample_items.distractor_logic: (6, 1), (12, 2), (18, 3) is the swap error; (1, 7), (2, 8) is additive.

sample_items.stem: Two points of a proportional relationship are plotted: (2, 4) and (4, 8). Your friend says the line between them should NOT be extended down to (0, 0). Is your friend right? Explain.
sample_items.answer: No. A proportional relationship always includes (0, 0) — zero of the input gives zero of the output — so the line does pass through the origin.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Agreeing with the friend signals the origin property isn't anchored; the picture shows the line heading straight for the corner.

vocabulary.definition: The grid where points are plotted using an x-axis (across) and a y-axis (up).
Two numbers in parentheses, (x, y) — across first, then up. The order matters.
The point (0, 0), where the two axes cross. Every proportional graph passes through it.
On a graph, a straight line through the origin — the picture of y = px.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid on the board (0 to 6 across, 0 to 12 up). Next to it, write the equation y = 2x and the story: 'Bananas cost $2 per pound.'
Give me three table rows for this equation — pick your own x-values and tell me each y.
Each row becomes an ordered pair: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6). The independent variable — pounds — always goes first. Say it as 'across, up.'
Plot (1, 2) while narrating: 'across 1, up 2.' Then hand the marker to the student for (2, 4) and (3, 6).
Watch the plotting order. A student who moves up first, or plots (4, 2) for the pair (2, 4), is swapping coordinates. Don't fix it yet — finish plotting and let the crooked point stand out.
Look at your three points. What shape are they making? If we lay a ruler along them, where does the line hit the edge of the grid at the bottom-left?
Straight line, through (0, 0). That's not luck — zero pounds of bananas costs zero dollars, and every y = px graph does this. Straight through the origin is the fingerprint of proportional.
Without plotting, is the point (5, 10) on this line? How can the equation answer that for you?

practice_problems.stem: Write the ordered pair for 'x = 4, y = 8.'
To plot the point (2, 6), how far do you move across, and how far up?
practice_problems.answer: Across 2, up 6.

practice_problems.stem: The equation y = 3x gives the miles, y, a hiker walks in x hours. Plot the points for x = 1, 2, and 4 on the grid, then check that they make a straight line through the origin.
practice_problems.answer: (1, 3), (2, 6), (4, 12) — all on the straight line through (0, 0).
practice_problems.notes: Blank grid — students plot. Watch for (3, 1) style swaps.

practice_problems.stem: Which point is on the graph of y = 6x: (2, 12) or (12, 2)? Explain the difference between them.
practice_problems.answer: (2, 12). When x = 2, y = 6 x 2 = 12. The pair (12, 2) swaps across and up — it would mean 12 hours for 2 miles.
practice_problems.notes: Head-on contrast of the swap error.

practice_problems.stem: Nia's equation is y = 5x (y = dollars earned for x chores). She plotted her point for 3 chores. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: Her math was right but her point is swapped. The independent variable (chores) goes first: the correct point is (3, 15) — across 3, up 15.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical coordinate-swap bait with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: The points (1, 4) and (3, 12) are on the graph of a proportional relationship. Name one MORE point on the line, and one point that is NOT on it.
practice_problems.answer: On: any (x, 4x), e.g., (2, 8) or (0, 0). Not on: any pair where y is not 4 times x, e.g., (2, 10).
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own on a shown line.

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph passes through (2, 5). Does it also pass through (4, 10)? Through (0, 0)? Explain both answers using the idea y = px.
practice_problems.answer: Yes to both. The rate is 5/2 = 2.5, so (4, 2.5 x 4) = (4, 10) is on the line, and x = 0 gives y = 0, so (0, 0) is always on it.
practice_problems.notes: Decimal rate — stretch tier — plus the origin property in the same breath.

practice_problems.stem: Sketch what the graph of 'a gym charges $10 per month' looks like, and explain why the graph of 'a gym charges $10 per month plus a $20 sign-up fee' would NOT pass through the origin.
practice_problems.answer: y = 10x is a straight line through (0, 0). Adding a one-time $20 lifts the whole line to start at (0, 20) — zero months already costs $20, so it can't pass through the origin and isn't proportional.
practice_problems.notes: Contrast case that previews why through-the-origin is the proportionality test.

activities.title: Human Coordinate Plane
materials: Masking-tape axes on the floor (0-8 each way)
activities.instructions:
1. Tape an x-axis and y-axis on the floor. Draw a rate card, e.g., 'y = 2x.'
2. Assign each student an x-value. They compute their y, then walk their point: across first, then up, counting out loud.
3. Once everyone is standing, run the string from the origin through the students. It should touch every person.
4. Debrief: why did the string start at (0, 0)? What happened to anyone who walked up before across?

activities.title: The Sideways Point
materials: Printed grid with Nia's flawed point plotted
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs plot the three correct points for y = 5x (x = 1, 2, 3) and lay a ruler through them.
2. They find Nia's point (15, 3) far off the line and diagnose why it missed.
3. Exit question: what do you SAY to yourself as you plot, so across and up never swap?

content.worked_problem: y = 5x for chores and dollars. Nia computed 5 x 3 = 15 correctly, then plotted (15, 3).
content.error_step: Nia put the dependent value first in the ordered pair — she plotted (y, x).
content.why: An ordered pair is (independent, dependent) = (across, up). Her point should be (3, 15); the swapped point lands nowhere near the line, which is how the graph itself catches the error.

activities.title: On the Line or Off the Line?
activities.instructions:
1. Post the graph of y = 3x. Partners sort each point card under 'On the line' or 'Off the line.'
2. Rule: every sort must be justified two ways — by the equation (does y = 3x work?) AND by the picture (does it sit on the line?).
3. Debrief: which check is faster? Which check would still work for x = 1,000?

strategy_links.why: Walking the floor grid makes 'across, then up' a physical habit before it's a plotted point.
A swapped point lands visibly off the line — the graph itself becomes the error-analysis tool.
Whiteboard pass with mini-grids lets the teacher catch coordinate-swappers on every single plot.

questioning_prompts: Which number in your pair is the independent variable — and which direction does it control, across or up?
Before you plot: say your point as 'across ___, up ___.'
Your three points are plotted. What do you expect them to form, and where should the line begin?
Is (0, 0) on this graph? What does that point mean in the story?
Without plotting, how can the equation tell you whether (7, 21) is on the line for y = 3x?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots the pair backwards — moves the y-value across and the x-value up, e.g., plots (8, 2) for x = 2, y = 8.
misconception_redirects.say: An ordered pair is (across, up) — the independent variable always rides first. Say it as you plot: 'across 2, up 8.' Now check: does your point sit above the 2 on the x-axis?
misconception_redirects.praise: Across first, then up — you plotted the pair in the right order and the point landed on the line.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student draws the line but starts it at their first plotted point instead of extending it through the origin.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask the story: what does zero cost? Zero pounds of bananas is zero dollars, so the point (0, 0) belongs to this relationship. Extend your line — does it hit the corner?
misconception_redirects.praise: You extended the line to the origin and said why — that's the fingerprint of every proportional graph.

quick_checks.prompt: Plot the point for x = 2 on the graph of y = 4x. Narrate as you go.
quick_checks.look_for: 'Across 2, up 8' landing at (2, 8). Landing at (8, 2) is the swap; plotting (2, 6) means the multiplication slipped.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: the graph of y = 9x passes through (0, 0). Defend your answer with the equation, not the picture.
quick_checks.look_for: True, because 9 x 0 = 0. A student reaching for a drawn graph instead of substituting hasn't linked the equation to its points.

worked_solution.stem: Bananas cost $2 per pound, so y = 2x gives the cost, y, of x pounds. Graph the relationship for x = 1, 2, and 3, and name the special point the line passes through.
worked_solution.answer: Points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6); the line passes through the origin, (0, 0).

steps.annotation: Use the equation to build table rows — every y is 2 times its x.
Each row becomes an ordered pair: independent variable first, (across, up).

steps.math: Plot: across 1 up 2, across 2 up 4, across 3 up 6
steps.annotation: Narrate the order as you plot — that's what keeps the coordinates from swapping.
The points line up straight and pass through the origin: zero pounds costs zero dollars. Straight through the origin is the signature of y = px.

faded_example.stem: A hiker walks 3 miles per hour, so y = 3x gives the miles, y, in x hours. Graph the relationship for x = 1, 2, and 4.
faded_example.answer: Points (1, 3), (2, 6), (4, 12) on a straight line through the origin.

steps.annotation: Build the rows from the equation.
Independent variable first in every pair.
Plot each pair, saying 'across ___, up ___' as you go.
Lay a ruler through your points. Where does the line cross, and why does the story make that point true?

sentence_starters: My ordered pair is (___, ___) — independent variable first, across then up.
The line passes through the origin because zero ___ means zero ___.

skills.name: Critique equations and claims about a proportional relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Write and use y = px from a real-world situation (skill 6RP5-S4)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A car goes 60 miles per hour. What equation gives miles, m, for h hours?

skills.i_do_script: Now we judge other people's equations. Watch me with 'a train travels 40 miles per hour': Student A wrote y = 40x, Student B wrote y = 40 + x. I don't argue about which LOOKS right — I test both with a real value. At x = 2 hours, A gives 80 miles and B gives 42 miles. Count it by hand: 40 miles the first hour, 40 more the second — 80. Student A wins, and I can say WHY B fails: adding 40 once ignores that the 40 happens every hour. A critique is a test plus a reason.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges an equation by surface plausibility ('y still gets bigger') instead of testing it with a value, so y = p + x gets accepted as proportional
canonical_error.example: For 'a plant grows 6 cm per week,' the student accepts y = 6 + x because 'the height goes up as weeks go up'
canonical_error.why: Both y = 6x and y = 6 + x increase, so 'bigger x makes bigger y' can't tell them apart. The student is missing the defining test of proportionality: y must be the SAME multiple of x every time, which addition breaks after the first step.

redirect_script.prompt: Pick x = 2 and run BOTH equations. Then count the real answer by hand from the story. Which equation matches the count? Now say why the other one misses.
redirect_script.praise: You tested with a real value and explained the miss. That's a mathematician's critique.

skills.item_template: A rate context plus one or two candidate equations (typically y = px vs. y = p + x, or a flipped/inverted equation). Student identifies the correct one and explains why the other fails, using a test value. DOK 3; calculations stay easy.

sample_items.stem:
A freight train travels 40 miles per hour. Two students wrote equations for the total miles, y, after x hours.

Student A: y = 40x
Student B: y = 40 + x

Which student is correct? Explain why the other student's equation is incorrect.
sample_items.answer: Student A. The train covers 40 miles EVERY hour, so the 40 multiplies x. Student B adds 40 only once: at x = 2 his equation gives 42 miles, but the train has really gone 80 miles.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who pick B usually reason 'it starts at 40 and grows' — plausibility judging instead of value testing.

sample_items.stem: Kira says the equation y = 6 + x represents 'a plant grows 6 cm every week' (x = weeks, y = total growth). Test her equation at x = 2 weeks and explain whether she is right.
sample_items.answer: She is wrong. Her equation gives 6 + 2 = 8 cm, but growing 6 cm each week for 2 weeks is 6 x 2 = 12 cm. The correct equation is y = 6x.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Accepting Kira's equation because '8 is bigger than 6' is the canonical plausibility error.

sample_items.stem: Which equation shows a proportional relationship between x and y?
sample_items.answer: y = 3x
sample_items.distractor_logic: The three foils all fail the through-the-origin/same-multiple test; y = 3x + 1 is the trickiest because it contains 3x. A follow-up: y = x/3 WOULD also be proportional — the form is y = px with p = 1/3.

sample_items.stem: A store sells rice for $5 per pound. Jen wrote p = 5c, where c is the cost in dollars and p is the pounds. Test her equation with 2 pounds of rice and explain her error.
sample_items.answer: Two pounds costs 5 x 2 = $10. Jen's equation says p = 5c, so for p = 2 it forces c = 0.40 — 40 cents for two pounds, which contradicts the story. She attached the rate to the wrong variable: cost depends on pounds, so c = 5p.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The flipped equation looks fine symbolically; only a test value exposes it. Students who 'fix' it to p = c/5 are correct but should connect it to c = 5p.

vocabulary.definition: y is always the same multiple of x — the equation has the form y = px, nothing added or subtracted.
Judging whether a claim is right by testing it and explaining the result.
An easy number you plug into an equation to see if it matches the real situation.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.RP proportional reasoning — constant of proportionality and percent applications.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'A train travels 40 miles per hour.' Below it: 'Student A: y = 40x. Student B: y = 40 + x.' (x = hours, y = total miles.)
Before any math — what does each equation CLAIM the train does? Read each one back as a sentence.
How could we settle this without arguing? What number should we test?
Pick x = 2 hours. Run both machines: A says 40 x 2 = 80. B says 40 + 2 = 42.
Now count the real answer from the story, hour by hour. After hour one, how far? After hour two?
If the student defends B with 'but it still goes up,' that's the plausibility trap. Ask: 'Both equations go up. Can BOTH be right? What does the hand count say?'
Student A wins the test. Now the second half of a critique: WHY does B fail? What did the '+' do to the 40 that the story doesn't allow?

Adding uses the 40 once; the story repeats it every hour. A full critique has both parts: the test result AND the reason. 'B is wrong because at 2 hours it gives 42, but the train really travels 80 — addition only counts the rate once.'

practice_problems.stem: A robot builds 5 toys per hour. Which is the correct equation for toys, y, in x hours: y = 5x or y = 5 + x?
practice_problems.answer: y = 5x

practice_problems.stem: Test the equation y = 9x at x = 3. What y do you get?
